title: New clothes
hook: beware of all enterprises that require new clothes (Walden 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, quiet desperation, and the line that follows it: wisdom does not do desperate things. Your line was not quietly desperate. Did one small, calm step get taken? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

New running shoes, a new planner, a new yoga mat still rolled in plastic. There's a particular hope that lives in a shopping bag. This time it'll be different, because this time there's equipment. Then the shoes sit by the door. The planner stops in February. Thoreau saw the same pattern in his own neighbors, with coats and hats instead of sneakers, and in the first chapter of Walden he wrote a warning that sounds almost like a proverb: beware of all enterprises that require new clothes.
screen: `HOPE IN A SHOPPING BAG.` → `THE SHOES BY THE DOOR.` → `A WARNING ABOUT CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: First, the whole sentence. It has two halves. Thoreau writes: "I say, beware of all enterprises that require new clothes, and not rather a new wearer of clothes." The second half is the point. The danger isn't clothes. It's starting with the outside and hoping the inside follows. If something real is changing, he suggests, it changes the person first, and the old coat will do fine for now. Second, the patch on the knee. Thoreau notices how much people fear being seen in old or mended clothes. He says that, for himself, nobody ever sank in his opinion for wearing a patch, but he suspects plenty of people would rather go into town with a broken leg than with torn trousers. It's a joke, and it isn't. We often guard our look more carefully than our lives. Third, fashion as a kind of faith. Thoreau teases how each generation laughs at old fashions and then follows the new ones with complete devotion. The tailor, he jokes, is treated almost like an authority on how a person ought to live. He's not angry about it. He's amused, and a little sad. Fourth, what this asks of a Tuesday. Not a vow to never shop again. Thoreau himself owned clothes and wore them. It's a small question to ask before any fresh start: does this need new equipment, or a new me? The run can begin in old shoes. The plan can begin on the back of an envelope. If the change is real, it will still be real in the old coat.
screen: `A NEW WEARER OF CLOTHES.` · `THE PATCH ON THE KNEE.` · `FASHION FOLLOWED DEVOTEDLY.` · `START IN THE OLD COAT.` · then, large: `NEW CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin something without buying anything. Settle, and breathe out slowly. Bring to mind a change you've been meaning to make. Notice if it came with a shopping list attached. Gear. An app. A book about the thing instead of the thing. Now, in your mind, set the list down. What could you do with exactly what you have, today, wearing what you're wearing right now? Let that one plain step come clear. The bell holds the time.
New clothes. Thoreau's warning in Walden: beware of enterprises that need new clothes, and not rather a new wearer of clothes. Change the person first; the old coat will do. Today's word.

Your line: no new clothes. Today, do one thing you've been waiting to start, using only what you already own. Old shoes, an old notebook, the clothes you have on. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of Walden use 'beware of all enterprises that require new clothes' as a check before a fresh start, beginning with what they already own.
